definition: The quality of being honest and sticking to strong moral principles, even when no one is watching.
example: A referee with integrity makes the same call no matter which team it helps.
nuance: Integrity goes beyond honesty: it means acting on your principles consistently, even when doing so costs you something.
prompt: A cashier realizes a customer accidentally overpaid by twenty dollars and has already left.
options: The cashier showed integrity by running after the customer to return the money.
The cashier showed integrity by keeping the extra bills and telling no one.
The cashier's integrity let her total long receipts in her head within seconds.
The cashier had the integrity to scold the customer loudly the next day.
reasons: Giving back money that isn't yours, even with effort, reflects firm honesty.
Quietly pocketing someone else's money is dishonest, the reverse of the word.
Quick mental math is a skill, not a sign of moral character.
Publicly embarrassing someone is rudeness, not principled behavior.

practice.prompt: A student finds the answer key to tomorrow's exam left on a classroom desk.
options: Thanks to her integrity, she blended easily into a new group of friends at lunch.
Her integrity was obvious from how nervous she always felt before exams.
Her integrity led her to hand the key to the teacher without peeking at it.
Her integrity led her to memorize every answer before anyone noticed.
reasons: Fitting into a group describes integration, a look-alike word, not moral character.
Feeling anxious says nothing about whether someone acts on firm principles.
Refusing an unfair advantage when nobody would know shows strong principles.
Secretly cheating is a failure of honesty, not an example of it.
